The third one would grab the person by the hair. They would turn in the direction of the Zinc Factory and they would kill those men by -- with a kind of machete, decapitating them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were involved in this killing operation?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't exactly tell. They all looked the same. They were wearing the same kind of clothing, they were more or less of the same age. There were between eight and ten of them. I don't know if this was done always by the same person, or rather the same persons, but they were there, lined up. And I couldn't tell you anything more precise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what the men who were doing the killings were wearing?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: This same kind of clothing; the one that was worn by other soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Camouflage clothing?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, camouflage clothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after you witnessed these first three men being killed, tell the Judges what happened.

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: The two soldiers went back, and they were bringing in other Bosniak men. And then a truck arrived, coming from the cornfield. And when the truck was filled with dead bodies, they had some kind of camouflage bags, they ordered some Muslims to fill up those camouflage bags, which were then put onto a truck. And they kept working like this for a while.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the truck with the bodies leave the area?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on several occasions, and it would come back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after the truck left the area, what happened?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: The truck would leave the area, and then it would come back again. The last time it came, it was already at dusk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Mr. Ademovic, how long was it that you watched killings take place from your location near the shed?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: It must have been, I'm not too sure, but it must have been two hours. More. More.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during this period of time, did you or your colleague, Mr. Karic, keep a count of how many people you had seen murdered?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Dzemal Karic had a box of cigarettes, Drina, from a Sarajevo factory, and he had a short pencil. And as they were taking them away, he was writing four, then five, then seven, and on. And then he added it up, and we got the figure of 83. But the pencil broke. Anyway, it was a stub only, so that it couldn't write any longer, and they were still taking people away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to estimate the number of people you saw killed in the fashion which you've described?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: What he added up was the correct sum, 83, but they continued taking people away, and then we could not write anymore. But there must have been over 100.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, please continue describing what occurred at that location.

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Night had already fallen, but it wasn't quite dark yet. I knew those people from sight. I didn't know their names. And the last batch, in it I recognised Hazim Lonjinac in that last group of five men. And then all of a sudden noise started, and those people came back alive, that group of five men. And they left. And we entered the Zinc Factory. And I found Hazim Lonjinac, who had been with that group, with a child in his arms. He's some kind of a son-in-law of mine. And I told him, "Son-in-law, I've already mourned you." And he said that an officer had come and attacked those Chetniks, and he gave me his name. And he said, "I was the one who got you away. Get down to the Zinc Factory." But I've forgotten the name. He gave me both the first and last name of that officer, but I've forgotten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to the assassins?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: They stayed there -- well, they left later on. As soon as they stopped killing, they just vanished.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the name of an individual who may be related to you by marriage, Hazim Lonjinac. And that's the man who you have identified as --

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, my niece -- he's my son-in-law. My niece is married to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to Hazim Lonjinac?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Don't I? My daughter-in-law told me, the wife of my son who was killed. My two daughters-in-law and my wife went towards Kladanj that night. And my daughter-in-law told me that she had got off the bus at some point, and several men were standing in a group next to a stone boundary. And when the headlights went on, then she recognised Hazim in that group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the location where Hazim was standing in that group?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see it myself, but from what my daughter-in-law told me, next to the asphalt, up the slope, next to the boundary, next to the bank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a name for that location?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Luke. Some people call it Luke. I've heard people call it Luke.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me return to the time when you came down from the hill and after you saw Hazim. Did you find your wife and your other family members in and around the Zinc Factory?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: No. And I never saw them again, until I arrived in Kladanj. And they had left that night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ademovic, I'd like you to describe, if you would, to the Judges the night between the 12th and the morning of the 13th. Can you describe the scene as you saw it?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: In the Zinc Factory compound -- nobody spent the night there, but across the asphalt, in the transport compound. And I was in the middle. All the people were around me. There was moonlight, and the visibility was better than now. And from all sides Chetniks were coming, carrying torches with them, flashlights. And people lying down were tired. They would pull the people up by the hair and look at their face. If they would like the face, they would take him away. If they didn't recognise him, they would leave him behind. But they mostly took them away. And people were screaming, people were distressed. It was awful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say, "The Chetniks were coming," can you be more precise? Who were the Chetniks? How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Chetniks. That was no army. Those are criminals. They are called the Bosnian Serb army, but that's a crime. They are beasts. They are not humans. A man, a human being, has a soul, and those people didn't have anything. Heavy crimes. What army?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were those individuals who came in in the night with those flashlights, how were they dressed? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: All military. I could have seen two or three in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ademovic, let me now turn to the morning of the 13th of July and focus your attention on the early morning hours. What did you do first thing in the morning of the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't sleep, nor did anybody else. The dawn broke and our heads hurt to a bursting point. Down there, there was the River Krizevica, and I started down to wash myself. There was no Chetniks around. And above me was a woman screaming like crazy, "What's happened?" They took away two of her daughters that night. I started towards the Krizevica, the stream. I washed my face, came back. I saw a man on his knees moving. This is cut [indicating], both his hands, around his ankles, also both feet, his nose cut off, his ears cut off, his eyes gouged out. He is moving on his knees and only moaning "Oh." He was hanging like that. I didn't come near him. Another one was hanging. I'm sorry. I didn't come near him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw two individuals, one of whom was mutilated and a second man who was hanging. Did I understand your testimony correctly?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. You understood me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do after you saw those two sights?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: I saw buses and I headed there straight away. I reached the rope, and they had separated -- many of us continued separating, so I reached the rope. It was tight there, but I bent down and passed under the rope, and nobody said anything. So I reached the bus, and its driver was an acquaintance of mine before the war, a fellow driver. So I sat next to him and headed for Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there for just a second. I omitted to show you three exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I'd like the usher to put these on the ELMO, Prosecutor's Exhibit 5/10, 5/13 and 5/11.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These relate to the killings that you described earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Which exhibit is that, please? THE USHER: 5/10.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise Prosecutor's Exhibit 5/10?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: I do. Where shall I show it? Here, this is Aljo's house [indicates]. This is also Aljo's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, let him use the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please point to Aljo's house, and then I'll describe it to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: This is Aljo's house [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: For the record, the witness has put the pointer on the house that is directly in the middle of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you go to Exhibit 5/10, please. I'm sorry, 5/13. Do you recognise that photograph?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: This is the stable. This is the shed where I was, from where I watched. Down here [indicates], down there, there should have been the Zinc Factory, but it's not here. Aljo's house is over there. That's where it should be. Between the Zinc Factory and the house, there was to be some wheat or some corn, and that's where the slaughter took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Just for the record, the witness indicated with his pointer --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- and would you point again where you were hidden when observed these events took, please? Just put the pointer on the ELMO where you were hidden?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The witness has put his pointer on the left-hand side of this structure. There appears to be some perpendicular wooden slats at the left side of that building, and that's where he said he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that also the location where Mr. Karic was?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Usher, could you place Prosecutor's 5/11 on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise anything in that particular photograph?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Here's the fence through which the Chetniks were taking away the Bosniaks, through this wire fence [indicates]. And this is Aljo's house. And that's where they took them through, and there should be the stable, but it's not here. I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now let me, for the record -- the witness, when he was talking about the fence, he was pointing to a fence that is on the -- more to the right side than to the left side. It appears to have a hole in it. And when he pointed and referred to Aljo's house, he was referring to the house, the roof of which is on the left-hand side. It's the tallest structure in the photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Ademovic. You can turn around and we can continue with your testimony.

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we get, Mr. Ademovic, to your actually leaving the enclave on a bus, let me ask you, did anybody, prior to your getting on a bus, come to you and give you a choice, as to whether you could stay in Srebrenica and Potocari, or whether you could go to any particular location you wanted?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: No way. All them, they were shouting at us, cursing us, cursing Aljo, saying, "Why didn't you go with Fikret? Perhaps you would have survived." Here, nobody -- no, we were all leaving, getting away from knives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you, please, tell me where you went. You said you got on a bus. Tell the Judges what happened when you got on the bus and who you recognised.

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: I only recognised the fellow driver, that one, and all those people there, I wasn't really looking. Perhaps I knew somebody, but I can't remember. I only remember the driver, Raco Madzarevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was a colleague of yours, or a former colleague; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: He was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me what happened.

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once you got on the bus.

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: I got onto the bus, I sat somewhere in the middle of the bus, and when the bus was full, he set off. When we passed by Bratunac, he called me to sit next to him and I sat next to him. He offered me a cigarette and said, "Well, how about you? Are your sons alive?" I said, "I don't know." "Where did you go?" And I said, "Through the woods." And he said "Not good. There was some bad fighting with our army and there was also some fighting between your troops. Lots of people died. I hope somebody is still alive. We were to take you tonight," Wednesday night, that is, "and I started and I was brought back from the petrol station at Zivinice, and I saw our troops moving to meet your troops to an ambush, so that I didn't drive last night, nobody drove last night." When we got to Sandici, Pantic called Milici -- militia men stopped us. Before the war, he was a policeman. And that man was lying there on the asphalt next to him, and there were about 20 through Sandici, 20 men in civilian clothes with their hands like that. Pantic shook hands with me and said, "Hi. I looked for you yesterday in Potocari. I was bringing you some Slivovitz, some brandy, but I couldn't find you. And now I don't have it with me. Go and sit in the back. Don't sit here. Raco, get those two lads, they're Muslims. They arrived through the woods. They were good to us." And we went on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you some questions to clarify your testimony. Who was Pantic? Was he a Serb?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: A Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know him -- you knew him from before the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we knew each other well before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that you saw 20 people. How were their hands? Could you show the Judges --

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Around 20, around 20.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Judges how they were positioned and what position their hands were in?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: They were all in civilian clothes, and they their hands like this [indicates]. Nobody was driving them down. They were coming down the hill by themselves, down to where Pantic is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And when the witness said "like this," he put both his hands together behind the back of his head, so the record is perfectly clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did Pantic put some people on the bus?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Two young boys, some 12 or 13 years old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why he put those young lads on the bus?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: I know nothing. I don't know the reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the bus then drive away from Sandici?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which direction did it drive?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Towards Konjevic Polje, Milici, Nova Kasaba, Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see anything unusual on the way to Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: I did. Before Kaldrmica, to our right, there were about two or three buses standing, and to the left, there were the Chetnik troops, so that Raco couldn't get through, and he stopped. And he turned his hand, and with his coat, he covered my head behind his back. And two soldiers approached Raco. Raco opened the door, "We want to see if there is anything for us," and he said, "There's nothing for you," and they turned back, that is, they didn't get onto the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: And I watched from the buses how they were taking off men, and there were some women. And the buses started, and Raco started towards the playground, near Nova Kasaba. Around 1.000 Muslim Bosniaks were walking in a column, with their hands like this [indicates]. And Chetnici escorting them with rifles. Raco was driving very slowly and said, "Bego, do you recognise anyone?" And I said, "I don't, not one," because I saw them from their back. So he stopped in Nova Kasaba, he honked, and a shop owner came out and Raco asked for a litre of brandy. And the grocer brought it to him, and he paid him, and he just dropped it in front of him and went on driving. And when we reached Luke --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you right there because I need to clarify a couple points in your testimony. You said you saw about 1.000 men. Could you tell if these men were Muslim men or if they were Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Muslims, and Bosnian Serbs were driving them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in which direction were they going? I'm afraid I missed that part of your testimony. Were they going in a particular direction, to a particular location?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Towards Kasaba, before the playground. That's what I saw. Towards Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "playground," what kind of a playground is it?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Football, a football stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Again, for the record, when this witness indicated that the men had their hands, again, in a particular position, he made a gesture for the Court to see, which was both hands behind the back of the head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ademovic, where did you stop that bus journey?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: At Luke.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened there?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: The troops there surrounded the bus, and Raco got out that brandy from the glove compartment and two big tins and said, "Bego, give it to that woman, to put it in her bag, and when you cross over there, have a drink. Had I known that I'd come across you, I would have brought some marks for you. I've got lots of Serbian money, but you can't use it over there." And I said, "Well, shall I cross alive?" And he said, "You will." And he opened the door, took me by my left shoulder and said -- he called the radio and said, "Vojvoda, call them on the radio and tell not to leave this one alone, he is our fellow driver," and the other one replied, "Nobody will touch Bego." And that's how I continued my journey.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some point in time, did you help a woman, as well?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: When I was leaving that bus, those troops, they shouted at me to come back asking, "Would I mind taking along a woman who had suffered a stroke?" and I said "Sure." So I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ademovic, while you were at Luke, did you see anything happen to a young girl?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: I did. I saw a Chetnik dragging her back. She had torn all her clothes. She could have been 18, 19, and she was screaming, "Uncle Bego, help me. Don't let them do it." But I kept silent, I wasn't saying anything, and he dragged her behind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that young girl?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't. She knew me. I didn't know her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as you made your way toward the free territory, did you see any Bosnian Serb soldiers you knew?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Two were sitting to the right of the road, and he said, "Bego, take his wife, she has suffered a stroke," and I've shared lots of meals with them in their house, so all right. So they said, "Bego, come sit down. Have some water. You'll faint." So I sat down, he gave me a box of cigarettes, and I had a brief rest, and that's how I went on my journey.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name or nickname of that particular soldier?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know his name. He used to work for the bauxite. That's what they called him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. I didn't hear what they called him. What did they call him?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Lega. That was his nickname or perhaps his last name. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Ademovic. I've concluded my examination. My colleagues will ask you some questions.

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, how long will you need for your cross-examination, more or less?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it will be Mr. Visnjic who will cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So I'm asking the same question of Mr. Visnjic. How long will you take? I'm asking because of the break. Should we make the break now or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I was about to suggest a break because we have to resolve some technical matters with the technical booth, so as to get ready for it, and I should like to suggest a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We shall now make a 15-minute break, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ademovic, we are now going to continue with your evidence. Let me just remind you that you have to speak slowly because we have interpreters here who are interpreting what you say, and you have to speak slowly. I hope Mr. Visnjic will do the same. And we'll also show you how to do it, how to speak slowly. Mr. Visnjic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Mr. Visnjic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ademovic, I know it is hard for you to be reminded of these events, but unfortunately we have to ask you a few details, we have to ask you to explain the events that took place in July 1995 in somewhat greater detail. Mr. Ademovic, could you please explain to the Chamber whether you have given any statement about these events on any previous occasion?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how many statements I gave to the Tribunal, but I remember giving a statement to the authorities in Tuzla on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ademovic, the usher will now show you Exhibit 6. Exhibit 6 is your statement of the 18th of August, 1995, the statement that you gave to the State Security Service in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can tell you all about it. I don't have to read it. I'll tell you how it happened. I was called in Tuzla, they told me to come to an office, which was a small office, a small room. There were four of us, three men and one woman. The investigators were not serious at all. They were not serious. So they were flirting with the lady, they were not listening to what I was saying. And at the moment I had to put my signature on the statement, he didn't bother to read it -- I'm sorry. He did read it. But I told him that the statement had nothing to do with what I had just told him, and he told me that I should sign it now, that they were very busy, that he would later on come to see me at home or call me to his office, and that we would correct the statement later on. He never came to see me, nor did he ever call me. But I was called by the Tribunal in Tuzla, so I told them that the statement that I had previously given was not correct, the statement that I gave to our SUP, Ministry of the Interior. But they told me that this did not matter, that what mattered was what I was going to tell them, and this is how we proceeded. So the original statement is not correct, and I warned them about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ademovic, were you ever called again?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: You mean by our people, by the SUP people, the people from Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you give one more statement to the Tribunal later on?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: I gave several statements to the Tribunal. I don't know how many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were giving your statement to the Tribunal, was anybody from the Bosniak police present on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: I gave the statement in the SUP, in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were giving the statement to the Tribunal, was anybody present, anybody from the Tuzla Ministry of the Interior, present in the office?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean, they were wearing uniforms. They were people from the SUP, people from the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ademovic, do you then deny everything that was said in the statement of the 18th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: I do not deny everything. There have been errors, that is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, sorry to interrupt, but I believe the witness has already answered that question. If you ask specific questions, you will get specific answers. I believe that the witness has already explained these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I was already going to ask a very specific question in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ademovic, let me read you a passage from your statement of the 18th of August, I mean, the statement you said was a bit problematic, and I should like to hear an explanation from you. I should like you to explain the differences from that statement and what you're saying now.

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please wait for my question.

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the interpreters, the Serbian version of the text is on page 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "In the meantime, I ended up in the Express Transport compound, from where I saw a Chetnik, blond, short, medium build, close to the asphalt road. He snatched a three-or four-month old child from its mother's arms and smashed it on the cement. He then took the woman by the hair, put her head across his knee and slit her throat. The two men from the crowd wrapped the corpses in a blanket and took them away along the Bratunac road."

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I don't know what he wrote down. This is what I heard later on. I heard that the woman had been Naser's close relative, that she was killed together with her child. But I did not say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but the event, the way you related it today, is not the same one that is described in the statement?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how it happened. I only heard people describe the event later on, how this Naser's close relative was killed, together with her child.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us about an event -- you told us about this event today, and you told us that a baby was killed by a soldier in the Zinc Company?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, this is not the same event.

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, these are two different things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean, "two different things"?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can only say that the child -- I can only claim that the child was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever mention this event, the way you described it today, to the investigative authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: I may have told them that I had heard about the event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I'm asking you about this particular one that took place near the Zinc Company.

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that I told them so.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Visnjic, but Witness, please, try to make a pause before you start answering the questions. This will be much easier for the interpreters. You speak the same language, the counsel and you, and I know that it is very easy for the two of you to communicate speedily, but you have to bear in mind that there are interpreters between you. If you can please bear this fact in mind, the Chamber will be grateful. I could perhaps motion to you, I can tell you either to slow down, like this [indicates], or to make a pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to remind the interpreters to say "Question" and "Answer" because sometimes it is very difficult to distinguish between the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Visnjic, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ademovic, let me read you one more passage from your statement of the 18th of August, 1995. It is the last passage on the first page of the Serbo-Croatian text. "When they left at around 1300, Chetniks went into the crowd and immediately began taking away young women. I was with Ibran Mehmic [phoen] and Dzemal Karic from Kasaba in the Zinkada compound, when I saw Chetniks taking away a group of about ten young women towards the river, which was across from the Zinkada. I do not know any of the young women, but I know that the group of Chetniks who took away the women was commanded by Zoran Mirosavljevic, son of Dimitri, from Bratunac."

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: I already told you that there were a lot of people there, and I told you that the people who took my statement didn't actually listen to what I was stating. They were flirting with this young woman. I don't know what they wrote down. This is not what I said, this is not what I saw, and this is not what I told them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ademovic, you described an event today in which a Serb soldier took away a Muslim girl from her parents.

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That took place in the Zinc Factory. There were two soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. That is the event I have in mind. Could you please tell us whether the event that you have described today and the event as it is described in the statement, if such an event should have happened, are one and the same event?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: I was just about to explain this to you. This is something different. This is not what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ademovic, I should like to go back to the 12th of July, 1995 and your whereabouts on that day. I think that the record shows that while you were near Aljo's house, that you reached that particular location at around 10.00, but I don't think it is correct.

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: No, this is not correct. I got there on Tuesday, at 11.00 p.m. I arrived in Potocari, in the Zinc Factory, on that evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. I should like to discuss the incident of the killing of a number of Muslims by Serb soldiers in the vicinity of Aljo's house. Do you know which event I have in mind?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When exactly did you reach the position from which you could observe the event?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have a watch, but it could have been sometime after 3.00, 3.00 p.m. Yes, it was in the afternoon hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give us an idea as to how long this event lasted?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether you followed my testimony. It was a bit -- it was between two and three hours. But I didn't have a watch, so I couldn't tell you more precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should now like to discuss a few details of that event, if you can remember them. You spoke about a kind of ramp. I more or less have an idea as to what you had in mind, but could you explain to the Judges what it was?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: There were two -- there was a kind of scaffold that had been prepared for the killing, and there was a beam across which people were put, with their hands behind their backs. The Chetniks were holding their hands behind their backs. There was a third Chetnik holding them by their head, and there was a fourth one who was chopping their heads off and throwing them on a pile.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said they used a kind of sword.

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, some people call it a sword, some people call it a knife. You probably know exactly what I'm talking about. Some people even call it a machete. We have hundreds of names for one particular thing in the Bosnian language.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but I believe that there is a difference between a knife and a sword and a saber. Could you please explain the difference to the Judges?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what more you want. There is this thing -- I must say that I didn't come close to those men. I had not had any sleep for five days because of the shelling, because of the commotion and everything, but I could see a huge blade like this [indicates] that they used for chopping off people's heads. I don't know exactly how you would call it. We call it, I don't know, a saber, a sword, a butcher's knife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know it's a bit uncomfortable for you to remember these details, but could you tell us how it happened, this chopping off of heads?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the same way -- they chopped off people's heads the way you chop off heads of animals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, what is the objective of your questions? I mean, how can we be assisted by these details?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness has mentioned the approximate time of the event, and he also gave us an approximate number of people that were killed in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Visnjic, but I think that we should be able to understand. We all realise that it is very difficult for a witness to be very specific and precise after five years, and we cannot expect the witness to tell the exact time of the day, the exact number of the victims. I don't think that these particular details are relevant for the present case. I do not wish to impose any method on you -- you're doing your job and I have a profound respect for that -- but we simply cannot ask this witness to remember things that took place five years ago, and he just told you that he hadn't had any sleep for five days. We have to be able to imagine the circumstances of the event, which was very emotional, and we have to bear in mind that there are certain limitations on human perception. I'm sorry, but I have to tell you that it is almost a torture -- I'm a bit reluctant to use this word -- for the witness, to try to remind him of all these events. Well, I don't want to say that you've been torturing this witness, but please bear in mind the fact that we have to proceed in a speedy fashion and we have to restrict ourselves to the details which are really important and relevant. Please try to be more precise and direct in your questions. And I'm sorry once again for having interrupted you, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ademovic, I'm now going to read a portion from your statement given on the 23rd of May, 1996, and I should like you to confirm this passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is Exhibit 7, page 3, last paragraph of the Serbo-Croat version.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This statement will be marked as Exhibit D7.

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Why don't you read it to me? I can't read very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "In between the executions, the group of soldiers was drinking and eating."

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "It looked like it was for them a kind of entertainment --"

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was like a wedding. They would drink and play amongst themselves in between two killings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "The same two soldiers went to fetch another group of men, and the same event happened again."

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they brought another group of men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ademovic, at what intervals would those two same soldiers go back to the Zinc Factory to bring new people? And how many men would they bring along with them?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, not less than four, not more than six or seven. Somewhere between four and seven.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did it take them to go and bring that group? Well, the Judge has just told you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Witness. Could we make something into a rule? Before you begin to answer, take one minute to think. Can you understand what I'm saying? So Mr. Visnjic asks you a question --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just imagine that you have to take one minute to think about your answer, and then answer. Okay? All right? Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't have a watch. I couldn't really time it. I couldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One more question, Mr. Ademovic, about that incident. You said that bodies were put in some camouflage bags, or something like that, if I understood you well.

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of sacks were they?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they are sky blue. They are more or less like this chair here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why camouflage? I don't understand. Was it something with the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's the colour, that's what I call it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is Aljo Hasanovic, Mr. Ademovic?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Aljo Hasanovic, the owner of the house. They were slaughtering next to his house. Aljo.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, do you have any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Riad. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Bego Ademovic, good afternoon. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I just want to follow with you some of this very painful experience you had. I will not prolong it, as much as I can. First you said, when I think the Prosecutor asked you about the Bosnian Serb soldiers, you said that that was no army. When you said that, I understood, or perhaps it was meant, that these were monsters and not soldiers. But did you also mean that they were not organised completely, they were just wild people running around, or was it disciplined as an army, although they were acting like monsters? Did you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: I understand your question. A proper army wages a war against an army and does not just kill, does not mutilate, does not rape the young girls, does not cut arms, does not gouge out eyes, does not behead people. So that to me, they're wild men. No army, they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes. Please bear with me. It so happened in previous wars, perhaps you were not born, there was the Second World War, where some armies exterminated people and they were still called armies. So do you consider that this was just bands, wild bands, or was it in the form of an army? I'm speaking from the formation side, not their morality. I understand your revolt, but we're not discussing their morality. So the discipline, the organisation, the weapons, and what constitutes an army officially.

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: The Chetnik leadership, the top, from Milosevic in Belgrade, organised something like a hoard of miscreants to exterminate the Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina, to create Greater Serbia. When such a case happened, I wasn't born then, but the same thing was in 1941. In my village, 73 people burnt to death in their houses, and 61 survived, and the tradition goes on. That's what my parents told me. I don't know. They killed my uncle and brothers and sisters. And what do I know? Lots of my relatives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Well, that brings me to another question, because you also mentioned that the soldiers, when they stopped you and cursed you and your group, they told you, "This is a Serb country." Did they tell you what you were supposed to do, where you were supposed to go?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: The soldier did not stop me. That was in Potocari. When they stopped us, they did not insult anybody, they did not offend anybody on the road. And this happened in Potocari, on Wednesday, after 10.00. They were cursing our balija mothers, "You'll all be butchered. You will be burned in acid. This is our Serb fatherland. This is Greater Serbia."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, when you were on your way to Konjevic Polje, I remember you said two soldiers asked the driver, Raco, when he stopped, they asked him, "Is there anything for us," if you remember. What did they mean by "Is there anything for us?"

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he meant if they liked somebody, they would get them off, so to kill them, to rape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: In fact, you also mentioned that sometimes, and you gave two different meanings, you said, "They would stop people and choose the people they liked to kill." What is the meaning of "choose the people they liked"? I remember your words. You said, "Sometimes the people they liked and sometimes the people they suspected." Does that apply to women or to men?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, women, if they liked them, to rape them, and men, to finish them off, unless somebody was a friend of theirs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I found your words. You said, "They would pick the people they recognised." Were they after certain people, or they just took anyone?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: That happened too, to look for individuals, for specific individuals, but that only happened now and then. They were usually taking everybody. In Potocari, there lived Omer. He was born like this [indicates], he was an invalid; he was 75 years old, and they killed him too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: If you remember, you mentioned that you saw something like 1.000 Muslims, driven by Serbs, with their hands behind their heads. I think that was when you were in the bus. Did you know after that what happened to these men?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Killed in the playground, before Kasaba, all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And how did you know that?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: People who watched it said, hiding in the thicket and watching from the thicket. Brought to the playground, put a table there, a PAM on the table, around the table, and they would just go around, make a round, and finish them all off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Also by slaughtering them with knives or shooting, or you don't know? You don't know the way.

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: I heard only about shooting them dead, not about slaughtering them dead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Just one last question. Perhaps I don't want to remind you. You said your mother died in the forest, in the woods. How did she die?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: My mother -- my mother was 81 and was over 100 kilogrammes. We were going through the woods -- we were going through the forest and she remained there, she died there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I would like to thank you and to apologise for having aroused these memories.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness Ademovic, I have only one question for you. Are you ready?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Witness Ademovic, you were a driver by profession, and it took you to large cities, especially before the war, on various occasions.

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For instance, you must have been to Sarajevo very many times.

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Sarajevo, was there a military barracks there?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I never went into the barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was there a police station there, for instance?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: In Sarajevo, you mean? Yes. Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the streets of Sarajevo, for instance, or perhaps some other city, could you distinguish between a soldier and a policeman?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: You mean before the war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the war, yes.

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. They had different uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They had different uniforms.

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 10th, the 11th, the 12th, the 13th of July, did you see the difference between the police and the military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: BEGO ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't. Those camouflage uniforms are all alike, and I know nothing about them. I knew what Tito's uniform was, but that was a different type of police and a different kind of army. Now I don't understand anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this was your answer. Thank you very much. We should like to thank you for coming to give your evidence. It is always difficult to bring back those memories, to remember those horrible things that you lived through, but we hope that having come here, it will help you to find peace for yourself and enough peace to live in peace with other people, whether with people of your religion, your race, or perhaps you will make some other choice. But perhaps you were not asked something that you should like to say, that you had no other opportunity to say. Is there something that you should like to say now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I hope if Alija goes from power, his party, and if Milosevic goes, then we shall live together as we did before. If they stay on, there will be no life for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much, and we wish you a happy return home.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, Your Honour, I want to see if Exhibits D6 and D7 are admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, do you want to tender these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Mr. President, yes. D6 and D7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Any objections? Mr. Harmon, do you object?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no objection to D6, and if you just give me one minute to look at D7, no objection to D7 either. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you know, Mr. Visnjic, the Prosecutor needs to look into it, to see if there is any obligation of confidentiality, if there is anything that requires different measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So D6 and D7 are admitted, and Mr. Dubuisson will take care of them. Very well. It is now twenty-five past two. I don't think that it is really possible to call in another witness, is it, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's up to Your Honours, Mr. President. We're prepared to present another witness, but I leave it to your discretion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Mr. Harmon. I do not really think it will be very convenient and useful to have a witness who will only take the solemn declaration and then leave. So we shall adjourn today, until half past nine tomorrow. I wish to apologise to the interpreters. I know the interpreters are well familiar with the working conditions, better than we do. We are really doing our best to help them, but there is -- spontaneity, I think, is more powerful, and I don't think that even the President of the Chamber can not interfere with the witness and the way in which he speaks. But we shall perhaps have to think of some technical device to keep us remembering the interpreters, that they are there. Very well. I hope that if we understand what their working conditions are, then perhaps we shall be able to do something about them and make them better. Very well. I wish you a pleasant afternoon, and we shall be back here at half past nine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: 2.38 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 30th day of March, 2000, at 9.30 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25
